stage1/problem/A1/v1:
Problem: In BMAD, pixel-level masks exist only for brain MRI, liver CT and RESC, while OCT17, chest X-ray and histopathology carry image-level labels only, so MVFA's mask-based multi-level alignment loss can learn from just half of its potential source data. Can MVFA's four adapter stages instead be trained with an image-level multiple-instance objective on the patch-to-text similarity maps — primary operator: top-k mean pooling of each level's patch anomaly scores, so an abnormal image must contain a small set of highly abnormal patches and a normal image none — using all source datasets with masks discarded, and (i) how much zero-shot image-level AUROC, pixel-level AUROC and PRO on the held-out modality is retained relative to mask-supervised MVFA, (ii) at which of the four feature levels localisation emerges under image-level supervision, and (iii) whether adding image-labelled-only datasets to the source pool compensates for the loss of masks? All results under the modality-disjoint leave-one-modality-out protocol with 3 seeds.

Rationale: The reviewers asked for a sharper novel element and a realistic trade-off. The novel element is twofold: the weak signal acts on text-anchored patch similarities at multiple ViT depths, which is not how weakly supervised segmentation is usually done (single-level class-activation maps), and it lets MVFA use source datasets that its current loss simply ignores. The label-budget question (iii) — more images with image labels versus fewer images with masks — is the decision a clinical site actually faces. The mechanism is fixed (top-k mean; max pooling and attention-MIL become ablations), the component is a single loss in the public MVFA code, and the evaluation reuses MVFA's metrics on BMAD under the shared modality-disjoint, multi-seed protocol, which keeps the problem feasible on one GPU. A negative result is still informative because it quantifies what pixel masks buy for cross-modality transfer.
stage1/problem/A2/v1:
Problem: Can MVFA be adapted to a new modality from an unlabelled pool of target scans — a source-free domain adaptation setting with no masks, no image labels and no curated normal support set — by self-training its adapters on pseudo-labels whose confidence is defined by agreement across MVFA's four feature levels (a pixel is pseudo-labelled only if all four levels' zero-shot anomaly maps place it in their lowest or highest 10% of scores), and how many unlabelled target scans are needed to match few-shot MVFA with K = 4 labelled images? Each BMAD target dataset is split 50/50 by patient (or by image where patient identifiers are unavailable) into an unlabelled adaptation pool and a disjoint test set; outcomes are image-level AUROC, pixel-level AUROC and PRO on the test half as a function of pool size N, against zero-shot and few-shot MVFA, under the modality-disjoint protocol with 3 seeds.

Rationale: Reviewers noted that self-training is familiar and asked for a medical, multi-level specific element and an actionable outcome. Cross-level agreement is specific to MVFA's design: its four adapter stages produce independent anomaly maps whose consensus is a natural, label-free confidence signal that generic self-training does not have, and it directly limits confirmation bias on unseen modalities. The 'unlabelled scans needed to match K labelled images' outcome gives a site a concrete decision. The explicit 50/50 split addresses the concern about small BMAD test sets, and including chest X-ray, where zero-shot performance is weakest, stress-tests whether bootstrapping works when pseudo-labels are poor.
stage1/problem/B1/v1:
Problem: Can a single anomaly threshold, chosen without any target labels, transfer to unseen modalities in MVFA's few-shot setting? MVFA's image score adds a zero-shot softmax probability in [0, 1] to a memory-bank cosine distance in [0, 2] with weight 0.5 and max-pools over pixels. We study a 2x2 design: (factor 1) branch scores raw versus standardised by each branch's leave-one-out patch-score distribution on the K normal support images (each support image's patches scored against the memory bank built from the other K-1 images, pooled over patches so that K = 2 is non-degenerate); (factor 2) max pooling versus top-k-mean pooling. In every cell the threshold is set as the 95th percentile of the support leave-one-out image scores. Outcomes: realised specificity and sensitivity at that threshold, F1, expected calibration error and image-level AUROC on every held-out BMAD modality, for K in {2, 4, 8, 16}, under the modality-disjoint, 3-seed, 3-draw protocol.

Rationale: The reviewers asked for one primary question, an explicit threshold rule, a fix for the K = 2 degeneracy and separable factors. The primary question is now threshold transfer; the support-set leave-one-out distribution supplies both the normalisation statistics and the threshold, which is the label-free element that distinguishes this from generic z-score fusion; the 2x2 design identifies the separate effects of normalisation and aggregation. Showing whether conclusions drawn from AUROC alone change at fixed operating points broadens the significance beyond MVFA. The study is inference-only on public MVFA checkpoints and therefore cheap to run across all seeds and draws.
stage1/problem/B2/v1:
Problem: Do conformal false-positive guarantees survive a modality shift for zero-shot CLIP-based medical anomaly detection, and can they be repaired without target labels? Using MVFA trained in the leave-one-modality-out setting, we calibrate a split-conformal threshold on normal images from the source modalities (pooled, and per modality with the strictest threshold taken) at nominal false-positive levels of 1%, 5% and 10%, and measure the realised false-positive rate and sensitivity on the held-out modality, for max-pixel versus top-k-mean versus 99th-percentile image aggregation. We then test a corrective variant, weighted split conformal prediction, in which each source calibration image is weighted by a density ratio between source calibration features and the unlabelled target test batch (estimated with a domain classifier on CLIP global features), and ask whether it reduces the coverage violation. Outcomes per held-out modality: realised FPR versus nominal level, coverage violation, sensitivity at the conformal threshold, and expected calibration error.

Rationale: The reviewers asked for precise calibration sets and nominal levels, positioning against distribution-shift conformal methods, and a corrective element. The calibration sets and levels are now explicit; weighted conformal prediction, the standard correction for covariate shift, is tested in the medical VLM setting using only the unlabelled test images that a zero-shot deployment necessarily sees. The problem stays fine-grained (only aggregation and thresholding change), inference-only and runnable on one GPU, and per-modality reporting makes the answer actionable: which shifts break the guarantee and whether the weighting repairs it.
stage1/problem/D1/v1:
Problem: Does explicitly modelling normality as compact improve MVFA's zero-shot transfer to unseen modalities? MVFA aligns patches symmetrically to one 'normal' and one 'abnormal' text anchor and stores raw support patches for few-shot comparison, so nothing in its objective encodes that normal tissue is compact while anomalies are diverse. We ask whether adding, at each of the four adapter levels, a set of M learnable normal prototypes trained jointly with the adapters on the source modalities — with a compactness loss pulling normal patches to their nearest prototype and a margin loss pushing abnormal patches away — improves zero-shot image-level AUROC, pixel-level AUROC and PRO on the held-out modality, and whether the learned prototypes, re-estimated from K normal target images, can replace the patch memory bank in the few-shot setting without loss of accuracy. Outcomes are reported for M in {8, 32, 128}, under the modality-disjoint, 3-seed protocol.

Rationale: The reviewers judged memory compression in the few-shot regime insignificant because the bank is small, and pointed to the more important question in G7 — modelling the compactness of normality. The problem is reframed accordingly: prototypes are learned jointly with the adapters on source data (not fitted post hoc as in PatchCore coresets), which is the element existing compression methods do not cover, and the few-shot replacement becomes a secondary outcome rather than the motivation. It is a contained change to the training objective in the public MVFA code and feasible on one GPU.
stage1/problem/D2/v1:
Problem: Is MVFA's frozen, template-averaged 'normal' text anchor a bottleneck for few-shot transfer, and can it be replaced by a support-conditioned normal anchor? First, as a precondition, we measure the sensitivity of MVFA's zero- and few-shot AUROC to the prompt templates (variance over 20 random subsets of 5, 10 and 20 of the 35 templates). If the text side matters, we replace the static normal anchor with one shifted towards the K normal support images — a light projector, trained on source modalities, maps the mean adapted feature of the support normals to an additive offset of the normal text embedding — while the abnormal side keeps several anchors (one per state description, matched many-to-one). Outcomes: few-shot image- and pixel-level AUROC and PRO on each held-out modality, and the template-sensitivity variance, under the modality-disjoint, 3-seed, 3-draw protocol.

Rationale: Reviewers noted that image-conditioned prompts already exist and asked for a different conditioning signal and an explicit hypothesis. Conditioning on the support normals, rather than on the test image, gives the anchor a modality-level notion of 'normal' without seeing anomalies, and the asymmetric many-to-one abnormal side addresses G7's distributional asymmetry. The sensitivity analysis is now a precondition that decides whether the second step is worth running.
